DEMO_CONVERSATIONS.title: Fix async race condition in cart checkout

messages.content: My checkout sometimes charges the cart twice if the user double-clicks 'Pay'. How do I stop that?
What about on the backend? Should I add idempotency there too?

Yes — always. Frontend guards prevent *most* double-clicks, but you should never trust the client alone for money-moving operations.

💡 Add an idempotency key generated once per checkout attempt (e.g. a UUID stored in the form) and pass it in the request header. On the backend, check if you've already processed that key before charging again:

```javascript
const existing = await db.payments.findUnique({ where: { idempotencyKey } });
if (existing) return res.json(existing); // already processed, return the same result
```

✅ This makes retries and double-clicks fully safe, even across network hiccups.
My useEffect keeps firing forever and I can't figure out why.
That was it, thanks! One more thing — should I add fetchData to the dependency array too?

This query takes 4 seconds on 200k rows:
```sql
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC;
```

Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on it first — but 9 times out of 10 with this pattern it's a missing composite index. You're filtering by `customer_id` *and* sorting by `created_at`, so a single-column index on just `customer_id` still forces a sort at query time.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
```

💡 Matching the index column order to your WHERE + ORDER BY lets Postgres walk the index in order and skip the sort step entirely.
Ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE — it confirms Seq Scan. Adding the index now, thanks!

Perfect, that confirms it. After adding the index, run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` again — you should see `Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_created` replace the `Seq Scan`, and the cost/time drop dramatically. ✅
My Node app container starts then exits with code 0 right away, no errors logged.

Exit code 0 (not a crash) with no logs almost always means the container had nothing keeping the process alive — usually the CMD ran a script that finished immediately instead of starting a long-running server.

Check your Dockerfile's CMD:
```dockerfile
# ❌ if this runs a one-off script instead of `node app.js`, container exits after it finishes
CMD ["npm", "run", "build"]
```
```dockerfile
# ✅ make sure the final CMD actually starts the server
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```
That was it — I had 'npm run build' as the last CMD instead of 'npm start'. Fixed now.

🎉 Glad that fixed it. One tip going forward: `docker logs <container>` right after a fast exit is your best friend — if it's empty, you're almost always looking at a CMD/entrypoint issue rather than an app crash.

DEMO_CONVERSATIONS.title: JWT vs session cookies — which for our API?

messages.content: Should our new mobile app use JWTs or session cookies for auth?

For a mobile app talking to a REST API, JWTs are usually the better fit:

✅ **JWT** — stateless, works naturally across app restarts, no server-side session store needed, easy to attach as a `Bearer` header.
❌ **Session cookies** — awkward on mobile (no browser cookie jar by default), and ties you to a server-side session store that has to be shared/replicated if you scale horizontally.

⚠️ If you do go with JWTs, keep the access token short-lived (e.g. 15 min) and pair it with a refresh token, rather than issuing a single long-lived token.
What about our existing web app — it already uses httpOnly cookies for the JWT.

That's actually a great middle ground for the web: you get JWT's statelessness *and* httpOnly cookies' protection against XSS token theft (JS on the page can't read the cookie). Keep that as-is for web, and just have the mobile app request the same JWT but store it in secure device storage (Keychain / Keystore) instead of a cookie, since mobile has no cookie jar to piggyback on.

DEMO_SNIPPETS.title: Python: context manager for timing
DEMO_SNIPPETS.description: Times a block of code using a with-statement.
DEMO_SNIPPETS.code:
import time
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def timer(label='block'):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    yield
    print(f"{label} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

# usage:
# with timer('db query'):
#     run_query()
